docs.title: Hours of video.Minutes to read.
docs.text:
youtube-to-docs turns any YouTube video, playlist or channel into searchable transcripts, Q&A that names who asked and who answered, summaries, infographics, audio briefings and WCAG 2.1 AA captions. One command, on the AI provider you already use.

Get started Watch the demo

$ uvx youtube-to-docs --help

Works with Gemini, Vertex AI, AWS Bedrock and Azure Foundry. Saves to CSV, Google Drive, SharePoint or Hugging Face.

docs.title: Everything said, everything shown. Organized.
docs.text: A transcript is only the start. Each video becomes a set of documents you can search, share, publish and listen to. Every file is listed in a CSV that opens in Excel or Google Sheets.

docs.title: Transcripts and SRT
docs.text: YouTube's captions, or a fresh speech-to-text pass with word timings and speaker labels from Gemini, Google Cloud or AWS.

docs.title: Q&A that names people
docs.text: Every question, who asked it, who answered, and a link that jumps to the exact second in the video.

docs.title: Summaries and tags
docs.text: A full summary, a one-sentence summary and topic tags. Write them from the transcript, or have Gemini watch the video itself.

docs.title: Infographics with alt text
docs.text: A one-page visual of the session, with descriptive alt text written by a model that looks at the image.

docs.title: Audio and video briefings
docs.text: The summary read aloud by a natural voice, and combined with the infographic into a short video you can share.

docs.title: Any language
docs.text: Transcripts, captions, summaries, Q&A, audio and video in a second language, translated by an LLM, AWS Translate or Google Cloud Translation.

docs.title: AI drafts it. People decide what's published.
docs.text:
Every output is a file you can open, check and change: transcripts, captions, speakers, Q&A and summaries. Edit them in a text editor, Google Docs or Word. The next run uses your edits instead of overwriting them.

How to edit outputs

docs.title: Fix the transcript once
docs.text: Correct a misheard name or a missing sentence in the transcript. Summaries, Q&A, infographics and audio you make afterwards are built from your corrected text.

docs.title: Review before you publish
docs.text: Nothing is published for you. Read the captions, summary and alt text, edit anything that's wrong, and delete any output you want made again.

docs.title: Auto-captions aren't compliant. These are.
docs.text: One flag, -cc, makes a video accessible under WCAG 2.1 Level AA and Section 508. It produces the files that public bodies, universities and publishers need, instead of the raw output of speech recognition.

docs.title: Corrected captions
docs.text: Timing is checked word by word against a second transcript. Misheard words, names, punctuation and missed speech are fixed. Every speaker is named on each change, using the name plates shown on screen. Lines are laid out at two 42-character lines over 1–7 seconds.

docs.title: Audio description
docs.text: Slides, chart figures, on-screen text and votes are described for blind viewers and fitted into pauses in the speech. You get WebVTT description tracks, a descriptive transcript and a video with the descriptions narrated.

docs.title: What the corrections look like
docs.text:
These lines come from a 2 hour 43 minute Maryland Senate budget hearing on the Departments of Information Technology, Labor and Commerce. The left column is YouTube's auto-captions. The right column is the -cc output, shown exactly as generated, with the changes in bold.

YouTube auto-captions Corrected by -cc Time Um we are first going to do the department of information technology this afternoon. Uh Yashadari Ry is our budget analyst We are first going to do the Department of Information Technology this afternoon. Yashodhara Rai is our budget analyst, 00:04:12 do it noted that it was working with the office of state procurement. DoIT noted that it was working with the Office of State Procurement. 00:06:28 103,000 service test tickets were received in fiscal 25. Of these 84% were resolved by force contact 103,000 service desk tickets were received in fiscal 25. Of these, 84% were resolved by first contact 00:07:05 >> Thank you, Senator Bailey. >> Thank you, Madam Chair. [Chair Nancy J. King] Thank you. Senator Bailey. [Sen. Jack Bailey] Thank you, Madam Chair. 01:10:55 I'm Stephan Covenant. I'm Stefan Komoniewski. 02:16:21 my name is Britney Eris Mendy My name is Brittany Arizmendi, 02:33:27

Names, agencies and acronyms are fixed using what's said and shown in the video, and the speaker is named every time it changes. Across the hearing, -cc made 2,492 captions and restored 5 lines the transcription missed. A meeting this long takes about 20 minutes and roughly $3 with the default models. You also get an Able Player page that opens straight from disk, so you can check the captions and descriptions before you publish.

docs.title: What the audio description looks like
docs.text:
The same run found the moments where something important is shown but not said, and described them. Short descriptions are spoken in pauses in the speech. Full descriptions go in the extended track and the descriptive transcript.

Spoken in a pause (00:00:08): "Text: Chair Nancy J. King, District 39, Montgomery County, Democrat."

Full description: A lower-third graphic reads, "Education, Business and Admin., Chair Nancy J. King, District 39, Montgomery County, Democrat."

Spoken in a pause (01:19:36): "A two-minute timer appears above Chair Nancy J. King."

Full description: A split-screen view shows Chair Nancy J. King speaking on the left beneath a two-minute timer, while Tim Walker sits at the witness table on the right.

More on captions and audio description

docs.title: A four-hour public hearing, made readable
docs.text:
These outputs come from a single run on a Maryland Senate Health and Human Services subcommittee session about COVID-19's impact on vulnerable populations. They are shown exactly as generated, without edits.

Infographic generated by gemini-nano-banana-2.1 from a gemini-4-argon summary. Image models can still misspell small text.
  • Speakers identified with their titles, such as Robert Neall (Secretary, Maryland Department of Health)
  • 24 questions paired with their answers and timestamp links
  • Summary organized by agency and by testimony
  • Alt text describing all seven panels of the infographic
  • Audio summary, tags and a one-line summary for the catalog

docs.title: Up and running in one line
docs.text:
No clone, no virtualenv. If you have uv, you can run it now. Pick the way you work:

Command lineClaude CodeAntigravityWeb appPython 
# Everything, best quality: summaries, Q&A, infographic, audio and accessible captions
uvx --with "youtube-to-docs[all]" youtube-to-docs https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=B0x2I_doX9o -a gemini-pro -cc

# A whole channel, summaries only
uvx youtube-to-docs @mga-hgo1740 -m gemini-3.5-flash-lite

Set YOUTUBE_DATA_API_KEY and GEMINI_API_KEY first (see Setup). Artifacts land in youtube-to-docs-artifacts/, and every option is in the Usage guide.

claude plugin marketplace add DoIT-Artificial-Intelligence/youtube-to-docs
claude plugin install youtube-to-docs@youtube-to-docs

Then ask: "Make the best accessible captions for https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=B0x2I_doX9o", or run /youtube-to-docs <url>.

agy plugin install https://github.com/DoIT-Artificial-Intelligence/youtube-to-docs

Then ask for what you want in plain language, e.g. "Save a summary of this video in Spanish".

uvx --with "youtube-to-docs[all]" youtube-to-docs-app

Open http://localhost:8000, paste a link and watch progress live. See the Web App docs.

from youtube_to_docs.transcript import fetch_transcript

transcript, is_generated = fetch_transcript("atmGAHYpf_c")
Optional extras and installing uv

Keep installs light by adding only what you need with --with "youtube-to-docs[extra,...]":

audio (download audio and video with yt-dlp) · video (build MP4s with ffmpeg) · workspace (Google Drive) · m365 (SharePoint and OneDrive) · aws (Bedrock) · azure (Azure OpenAI) · gcp (Gemini, Vertex AI and Google Cloud speech) · app (web app) · all (everything)

Install uv:

  • macOS/Linux: curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
  • Windows: powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"

docs.title: How This Works
docs.text: youtube-to-docs takes a YouTube video, playlist or channel and turns each video into a set of documents: a transcript, speakers, Q&A, summaries, tags, an infographic, an audio summary and, with -cc, accessible captions and audio description. Every output is saved as a file and listed in one CSV.

docs.title: Watch the overview
docs.text:
Your browser can't play this video. Download the explainer video (MP4). Transcript of the video

How youtube-to-docs works

youtube-to-docs turns videos into documents to search, share and hear. Here's how it works, in six steps.

1. Point it at YouTube

Start with a video link, a video ID, a playlist or a whole channel. Playlists and channels are expanded, and each video runs in turn.

2. Get the words

Next, it gets the words. By default, it uses YouTube's own captions. Or it transcribes the audio again with Gemini, Google Cloud or AWS. That gives real word timings and speaker labels. Either way, you get a transcript and a timed SRT file.

3. Let the model read

Then a language model of your choice reads the transcript. It can run on Gemini, Vertex AI, AWS Bedrock or Azure Foundry. It names the speakers and their titles. It pairs each question with its answer and a timestamp link. It writes a summary, a one-sentence summary and topic tags. Gemini can also watch the video, to read slides and name plates.

4. Turn it into media

From the summary, it can draw an infographic. Another model looks at the image and writes its alt text. It can read the summary aloud, and combine both into a video. And it can make everything again in a second language.

5. Make the video accessible

Add the -cc flag to make the original video accessible. Captions are corrected, and each speaker is named. They meet WCAG 2.1 Level AA and Section 508. Slides and on-screen text are described for blind viewers.

6. You stay in control

Every output is a file that you can review and edit. Run it again, and the later steps use your edits. A CSV lists every file and what each step cost. Save it all to your computer, Google Drive, SharePoint or Hugging Face.

Get started

Run it from the command line, the web app, or as a plugin for your AI assistant. One command takes you from a link to a full set of documents.

docs.title: The pipeline at a glance
docs.text:
1. Point it at YouTube. A video URL or ID, a playlist, an @channel, or a comma-separated list.
  2. Get the words. YouTube's captions, or a fresh speech-to-text transcript with word timings and speaker labels. Either way you get a transcript and an SRT file.
  3. Let the model read. An LLM on Gemini, Vertex AI, AWS Bedrock or Azure Foundry writes the speakers, Q&A, summaries and tags.
  4. Turn it into media. An infographic with alt text, an audio summary, a video that combines them, and translations.
  5. Make the video accessible. -cc writes corrected WCAG 2.1 AA captions and an audio description.
  6. You stay in control. Every output is a file you can edit, saved locally or to Google Drive, SharePoint or Hugging Face, with costs in the CSV.

Each step checks for its output before it runs, so a second run only does what's missing and keeps your edits.

docs.title: 1. Input
docs.text:
The entry point (youtube_to_docs/main.py) accepts:

Input Example Video URL https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=atmGAHYpf_c Video ID atmGAHYpf_c Playlist PL8ZxoInteClyHaiReuOHpv6Z4SPrXtYtW Channel handle (its Uploads playlist) @mga-hgo1740 Comma-separated list KuPc06JgI_A,GalhDyf3F8g

youtube_to_docs.transcript.resolve_video_ids uses the YouTube Data API to expand playlists and channels into their videos, which are then processed one at a time.

docs.title: 2. Transcripts
docs.text:
-t / --transcript chooses where the words come from:

  • YouTube (default): the video's existing captions, either uploaded or automatic. Automatic captions come from speech recognition, so they can contain errors, and they aren't always available straight away.
  • Speech-to-text: an AI model name (e.g. gemini-3.5-transcribe, gcp-chirp3, aws-transcribe) downloads the audio with yt-dlp and transcribes it again.

Both give a plain-text transcript and an .srt file with timings. The SRT is used later to put timestamps on the Q&A and to make corrected captions.

Speech-to-text details
  • gemini-3.5-transcribe is Google's dedicated speech-to-text model. It's called with a transcription config that asks for word timestamps and speaker diarization, so the SRT is built from real word offsets rather than times the model guessed, with [Speaker N] labels on speaker changes. Audio over 15 MB is uploaded with the Gemini Files API and deleted afterwards. The API reports audio input tokens but not transcript output tokens, so the STT cost column covers the input side only.
  • Other Gemini models (e.g. gemini-3.5-flash-lite) can be prompted to transcribe too.
  • gcp- models (Cloud Speech-to-Text V2) need GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT; YTD_GCS_BUCKET_NAME is recommended.
  • aws-transcribe needs YTD_S3_BUCKET_NAME.
  • With an AI transcript, a second summary is also written from the YouTube transcript for comparison. --no-youtube-summary skips it.

docs.title: 3. Text outputs
docs.text:
-m / --model chooses the LLM (youtube_to_docs/llms.py). The prefix picks the provider:

Provider Prefix Example Google Gemini and Gemma gemini-, gemma- gemini-3.5-flash-lite (the default for a bare -m) Google Cloud Vertex AI vertex- vertex-claude-haiku-5-5 AWS Bedrock bedrock- (or a bare claude- or nova-) bedrock-claude-haiku-5-5, bedrock-gpt-6-luna Azure Foundry foundry- foundry-gpt-6-luna

OpenAI GPT models on Bedrock are called through the Bedrock Mantle Chat Completions endpoint. A comma-separated list runs several models side by side, each with its own columns.

For each video, the model writes:

Output Made from Contents Speakers Transcript Each speaker's name and title or role Q&A Transcript, speakers and the SRT A table of Questioner, Question, Responder, Answer, Timestamp and a timestamp link to that second of the video Summary Transcript and video details A Markdown summary One-sentence summary Summary One sentence for a catalog or listing Tags Summary Up to 5 comma-separated topic tags Chapters The SRT One MM:SS Title line per section, following YouTube's chapter rules (first at 00:00, at least 3, each 10+ seconds) Description Summary, chapters and tags A plain-text YouTube description (no Markdown, ready to paste): a short description, Chapters:, then the tags as hashtags

The SRT is passed with the Q&A prompt as a timing reference, so each answer's timestamp comes from the captions' real timings rather than a guess.

docs.title: Model suites
docs.text:
-a / --all sets the text model, transcript, infographic and voice in one go:

Suite Text model Transcript Infographic Voice gemini-flash gemini-3.5-flash-lite gemini-3.5-flash-lite gemini-nano-banana-2.1 gemini-3.8-flash-lite-tts-Kore gemini-pro gemini-4-argon gemini-4-argon gemini-3-pro-image gemini-3.8-flash-tts-Kore gemini-flash-pro-image gemini-3.5-flash-lite gemini-3.5-flash-lite gemini-3-pro-image gemini-3.8-flash-lite-tts-Kore gcp-pro gemini-4-argon gcp-chirp3 gemini-3-pro-image gcp-chirp3 anthropic-opus claude-opus-5-5 (Bedrock) aws-transcribe gemini-3-pro-image aws-polly-Ruth

docs.title: Video understanding (--from-video)
docs.text:
--from-video agentic|static (or agentic,static) sends the YouTube URL to Gemini through the Interactions API, without downloading the video. Gemini writes a summary, one-sentence summary, speakers, Q&A and on-screen context (video-context-files/) from the video itself, so it can use slides, charts and name plates that a transcript misses. These are saved next to the transcript-based outputs under the source video-agentic or video-static, and get infographics and audio too.

  • Agentic (Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite and later, e.g. gemini-3.8-flash, gemini-4-argon): the model moves around the video, loading transcript, frames or audio only when it needs them. Works on multi-hour videos.
  • Static: frames are sampled at 1 FPS for the whole video. Limited to videos that fit in the model's context window (about 3 hours at the default resolution).

The first request loads the video, and later requests continue the same server-side session. Requests run in the background and are polled, with a 30-minute timeout. Costs include the model's reasoning (thought tokens) and the content it loads (tool use tokens). The transcript-based pipeline still runs alongside.

docs.title: 4. Media and translation
docs.text:
Flag Output Details -i / --infographic One infographic per summary, in infographic-files/ Gemini (gemini-3-pro-image for a bare -i, gemini-nano-banana-2.1, gemini-3.1-flash-lite-image) or Azure Foundry GPT Image 2.5 (foundry-gpt-image-2.5-sunburst, foundry-gpt-image-2.5-flare). 16:9 landscape at the model's highest resolution, so it works as a thumbnail. The prompt (video title and summary) is saved in infographic-prompts/. --alt-text-model Alt text for each infographic, in infographic-alt-text/ A multimodal model looks at the image itself and describes its layout and content. Defaults to the summary model. Prefixes such as "Alt text:" are removed. --tts The summary read aloud, in audio-files/ Gemini TTS (e.g. gemini-3.8-flash-lite-tts-Kore), Google Cloud (gcp-chirp3) or Amazon Polly (aws-polly-Ruth). --combine-infographic-audio An MP4 of the infographic with the audio, in video-files/ Made with static-ffmpeg, so there's no FFmpeg to install. Scaled to fit 3840×2160.

See Performance for how long each image model takes and what it costs.

docs.title: Translation
docs.text:
--translate {model}-{language} (e.g. gemini-3.5-flash-lite-es) makes every output again in a second language. Use aws-translate-{language} or gcp-translate-{language} to translate with AWS Translate or Google Cloud Translation instead of an LLM. Long texts are split to fit each service's limits.

Everything is made in English first, then for the target language:

  1. Transcript and SRT: YouTube's transcript in that language if there is one, otherwise the English transcript and SRT are translated.
  2. Summaries, Q&A and tags: written again from the translated transcript with the same model.
  3. Infographic, audio and video: made in both languages when -i, --tts or --combine-infographic-audio are set.

File names end in ({model}-{language}), e.g. (gcp-translate-es), to show how they were translated. CSV columns use the shorter (es).

docs.title: 5. Accessibility
docs.text:
-cc / --corrected-captions makes the original video accessible under WCAG 2.1 Level AA and Section 508. Without a value it uses gemini-4-argon-gemini-3.5-transcribe: the audio is transcribed with gemini-3.5-transcribe (unless -t is set) and the captions are corrected with gemini-4-argon. The format is {model} or {model}-{source}, e.g. gemini-4-argon-youtube.

Captions (SRT in srt-files/, a plain-text transcript in transcript-files/, and WebVTT in vtt-files/):

  1. Timing. The source SRT is aligned word by word with a second transcript of the same audio (YouTube's captions, or the STT transcript when correcting YouTube's), and cues with broken timestamps are re-timed.
  2. Speakers. Every cue is given a speaker, in windows of about 20 minutes, from diarization labels, the second transcript's speaker changes and the on-screen context: names and titles read from name plates, with the times each person is seen speaking. With Gemini, this context comes from one agentic request to the video, unless --from-video already made it.
  3. Text. Sections are corrected in parallel against the second transcript and the on-screen spellings: misheard words and names, punctuation, fillers, non-speech sounds and missed speech. The model edits text by cue ID and never writes timestamps, so long videos can't drift out of sync.
  4. Layout. Words are laid out as captions of at most two 42-character lines over 1–7 seconds, broken at sentence and clause boundaries, with [Name] on each change of speaker and no overlapping cues.

Audio description: scene changes in the downloaded video are described by the model from the frames and nearby dialogue, and fitted into pauses in the speech. The descriptions are saved as WebVTT description tracks (vtt-files/, standard and extended) and a descriptive transcript (descriptive-transcript-files/).

video-files/ gets the original video and a copy with the captions burned in and the descriptions narrated. vtt-files/ also gets an Able Player page for checking the tracks in a browser, and a self-contained version that streams the video from YouTube, for pasting into a site such as Google Sites. See Corrected Captions and Audio Description for the options.

docs.title: 6. Review, storage and cost
docs.text:
People have the final say. Every output is a file, or a Google Doc or Word file on Drive or SharePoint. When a step finds its output already exists, it reads it back instead of making it again, so later steps use any edits you've made, such as a corrected transcript. To make an output again, delete it. See Review and edit the outputs.

Storage. -o / --outfile chooses where the CSV and files go:

Value Saves to A file path (default youtube-to-docs-artifacts/youtube-docs.csv) Your computer workspace / w, or a folder ID Google Drive, folder youtube-to-docs-artifacts sharepoint / s SharePoint or OneDrive, folder youtube-to-docs-artifacts hf A Hugging Face dataset (--hugging-face-dataset) memory / m Memory only, with no files on disk (used by the web app) none / n Nowhere; results are only in the log

Storage is abstracted in youtube_to_docs/storage.py (LocalStorage, GoogleDriveStorage, M365Storage, HuggingFaceStorage, MemoryStorage, NullStorage), so the rest of the pipeline doesn't depend on where files go.

Cost. Every API call's token usage is priced from youtube_to_docs/prices.py, and the cost of each step (speakers, Q&A, summary, tags, transcription, infographic, alt text and corrected captions) is saved in its own CSV column. See Pricing.

docs.title: Interfaces
docs.text: The CLI, MCP server and web app all run the same main() pipeline.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
youtube-to-docs <url> [options]

Run youtube-to-docs --help for every option, or see the Usage Guide.

docs.title: MCP Server
docs.text: youtube_to_docs/mcp_server.py exposes a process_video tool over the Model Context Protocol, so AI assistants such as Claude can run the pipeline. It's included in the Claude Code and Antigravity plugin; see MCP Server to install it.

docs.title: Web App
docs.text:
A FastAPI app (youtube_to_docs/app.py) gives a browser form for submitting videos and watching progress:

youtube-to-docs-app
# App available at: http://localhost:8000
Endpoint Purpose POST /api/process Submits a job and returns a job_id GET /api/jobs/{job_id} Job status, output log and artifact list GET /api/jobs/{job_id}/stream Job output in real time (Server-Sent Events) GET /api/artifacts/{path} Downloads an artifact GET /api/model-suites The model suites

Jobs run in the background with asyncio.to_thread, and artifacts are collected from the output folders when a job finishes.

docs.title: Output folder
docs.text:
The CSV (written with polars) has a row per video, with its details, the path to every file and each step's cost. The files are organized by type:

youtube-to-docs-artifacts/
├── youtube-docs.csv              # One row per video: details, file paths, costs
├── transcript-files/             # Plain-text transcripts, including the corrected captions (-cc)
├── srt-files/                    # Timed SRT transcripts, including the WCAG 2.1 AA / Section 508 corrected captions (-cc)
├── audio-files/                  # Downloaded audio (for speech-to-text) and audio summaries
├── speaker-extraction-files/     # Speakers and their titles
├── qa-files/                     # Q&A tables with timestamp links
├── summary-files/                # Markdown summaries
├── summary-prompts/              # The exact prompts sent for each summary
├── one-sentence-summary-files/   # One-sentence summaries
├── tag-files/                    # Topic tags
├── chapter-files/                # YouTube chapters (MM:SS Title per line)
├── descriptions-files/           # Plain-text YouTube descriptions: description, chapters, hashtags
├── video-context-files/          # On-screen context from the video (--from-video, -cc)
├── infographic-files/            # Infographic images
├── infographic-prompts/          # The exact prompts sent for each infographic
├── infographic-alt-text/         # Alt text for each infographic
├── vtt-files/                    # WebVTT captions, description tracks and the Able Player page (-cc)
├── descriptive-transcript-files/ # Dialogue plus visual descriptions (-cc)
└── video-files/                  # Infographic + audio videos, and the captioned, described video (-cc)

docs.title: About the explainer video
docs.text:
The video at the top of this page was made from code in scripts/docs/explainer/build.py. The slides are HTML rendered by headless Chrome, so the text on screen is exact. The narration is read one sentence at a time by Gemini TTS (gemini-3.8-flash-tts, voice Kore), so each caption is timed to its sentence exactly. To change the video, edit the slides or narration in that file and run:

uv run --extra all scripts/docs/explainer/build.py

docs.title: Summaries
docs.text:
How long each model takes to summarize the same transcript, and what it costs. The test uses the YouTube transcript of atmGAHYpf_c, about 38,000 input tokens. Claude models count tokens differently, so they report more input tokens for the same text.

  • Time is the wall-clock time for one generate_summary call. failed means the call failed or the provider wasn't configured.
  • Cost is in USD, from the token counts and the prices on the Pricing page.

To re-run it, see scripts/performance.

Measured on 2026-10-19.

docs.title: Infographics
docs.text:
How long each image model takes to draw an infographic from the same summary, and what it costs. The summary is of the same video, written by gemini-3.5-flash-lite (the default -m model). Each model runs at its default: 16:9 landscape at the highest resolution it supports, with high thinking for Gemini.

  • Time is the wall-clock time for one generate_infographic call. failed means the call failed or the provider wasn't configured.
  • Cost is in USD, from the token counts and the prices on the Pricing page.
  • Size is the width and height of the image in pixels. gemini-3.1-flash-lite-image only supports 1K.

Measured on 2026-10-19.

Model Time Cost Size (pixels) gemini-3.1-flash-lite-image 8.5 s $0.12 1376 × 768 gemini-3-pro-image 40.2 s $0.50 5504 × 3072 gemini-nano-banana-2.1 49.1 s $0.22 5504 × 3072 foundry-gpt-image-2.5-flare 65.8 s $0.40 3840 × 2160 foundry-gpt-image-2.5-sunburst 88.1 s $0.40 3840 × 2160

gemini-3-pro-image, the default for -i, was the only model with no text errors on both videos we compared (this one and a 3h49m hearing). Image models can still misspell words, so check the text before you publish an infographic. Select an image to open the preview at full width.

gemini-3-pro-image: Default for -i. Clear 16:9 layout with no text errors found.

gemini-nano-banana-2.1: Bold, large headline numbers that stay readable as a thumbnail.

gemini-3.1-flash-lite-image: Fastest and cheapest, but 1K only, with some garbled and repeated text.

foundry-gpt-image-2.5-flare: The most detail, including speakers and their roles, in a dense layout.

foundry-gpt-image-2.5-sunburst: The most polished, poster-like design, but with several misspellings.

docs.title: Pricing
docs.text:
youtube-to-docs is free and open source. You pay only your AI provider, at their list prices, and every run records its estimated cost in the output CSV. Prices last updated 2026-10-19.

Summarize a 1-hour video Real run: a 3h49m hearing$1.01Gemini 4 Argon: speakers, Q&A, summary, tags and an infographic Transcribe an hour of audio

docs.title: What a video costs
docs.text:
The estimated cost of one summary pass over a video's transcript for each text model. Move the slider to match your video's length.

Video length 1 hour How the estimate works

A summary pass sends the whole transcript and gets about 2,000 tokens back. Transcripts run about 200 tokens per minute of speech; the benchmark video is 3h11m and 37,663 tokens. A full run makes several passes (speakers, Q&A, summary, one-sentence summary and tags), and Q&A also sends the timed captions, so a full text run costs roughly 4–5 times one pass. Claude models count about a third more tokens for the same text.

docs.title: Price list
docs.text:
Units, conversions and sources
  • Token prices are USD per 1 million tokens. Cached input applies when the same prompt prefix is reused.
  • Speech-to-text, text-to-speech and translation services are shown in the vendor's own unit (per minute or per 1M characters). The CLI converts them to token equivalents (about 4 characters or 0.2 seconds of audio per token) to estimate costs.
  • The per hour estimates assume 150 spoken words (about 900 characters) a minute, and that Gemini audio uses 32 tokens per second.
  • Infographic costs were measured on a real run at the default settings (the highest resolution each model supports, and high thinking for Gemini) and include the image prompt.
  • Prices come from the vendors' pricing pages and llm-prices.com, and they live in youtube_to_docs/prices.py, which is the same file the CLI uses. Spot a stale price? Open an issue.

docs.title: Usage Guide
docs.text: youtube-to-docs turns a YouTube video, playlist or channel into documents: a transcript, speakers, Q&A, summaries, tags, an infographic, an audio summary and, with -cc, accessible captions and audio description. It's a command-line tool, and it also runs as a web app, an MCP server and a Python library.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Install uv:

    macOS/LinuxWindows 
    curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

    powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"

  2. Set YOUTUBE_DATA_API_KEY and GEMINI_API_KEY (see Environment variables).

  3. Run it on a video:

    uvx --with "youtube-to-docs[all]" youtube-to-docs https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=atmGAHYpf_c -m

This saves the transcript, speakers, Q&A, tags and summaries to youtube-to-docs-artifacts/, and lists them in youtube-to-docs-artifacts/youtube-docs.csv.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Run the tool with uvx, so there's nothing to install apart from uv:

uvx youtube-to-docs --help

The base package fetches YouTube transcripts and metadata and saves to local files. Other features are optional extras. Add them with --with:

uvx --with "youtube-to-docs[audio,video]" youtube-to-docs ...
uvx --with "youtube-to-docs[all]" youtube-to-docs ...
Extra Needed for Installs audio Recommended. Downloading audio and video from YouTube (AI transcription, -cc) yt-dlp[default], deno video Making video files (-cia, -cc) static-ffmpeg gcp Gemini, Gemma and Vertex AI models, and Google Cloud speech, TTS and translation google-genai, google-cloud-speech, google-cloud-storage, google-cloud-texttospeech, google-cloud-translate aws AWS Bedrock, Transcribe, Polly and Translate boto3, botocore[crt] azure Azure Foundry models openai workspace Saving to Google Drive google-auth-oauthlib, pypandoc, pypandoc_binary m365 Saving to SharePoint or OneDrive msal, fastexcel, xlsxwriter, pypandoc, pypandoc_binary huggingface Saving to a Hugging Face dataset huggingface_hub app The web app fastapi, uvicorn all All of the above

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
Set the variables for the providers you use.

Variable Needed for YOUTUBE_DATA_API_KEY Video metadata, playlists and channels (YouTube Data API v3) GEMINI_API_KEY Gemini and Gemma models (gemini-…, gemma-…), including gemini-3.5-transcribe and Gemini TTS PROJECT_ID Vertex AI models (vertex-…). VERTEX_LOCATION sets the region (default global for newer Claude models, otherwise us-east5). GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT GCP Speech-to-Text (-t gcp-chirp3). YTD_GCS_BUCKET_NAME sets the bucket for temporary audio (default youtube-to-docs). AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK AWS Bedrock models (bedrock-…) YTD_S3_BUCKET_NAME AWS Transcribe (-t aws-transcribe), for temporary audio AZURE_FOUNDRY_ENDPOINT, AZURE_FOUNDRY_API_KEY Azure Foundry models (foundry-…) HF_TOKEN Saving to Hugging Face (-o hf) YTD_CC_WORKERS Optional. Parallel -cc requests (default 6). Lower it if you hit rate limits.

Google Cloud services (Speech-to-Text, Cloud TTS, Translation) use Application Default Credentials, and AWS services other than Bedrock use your usual AWS credentials.

docs.title: Google Drive and SharePoint sign-in
docs.text:
You only need this to save outputs to Google Drive (-o workspace) or SharePoint/OneDrive (-o sharepoint).

Google Drive. Save your Google Cloud OAuth 2.0 client secret as ~/.google_client_secret.json:

{
  "installed": {
    "client_id": "YOUR_CLIENT_ID.apps.googleusercontent.com",
    "project_id": "your-project-id",
    "auth_uri": "https://accounts.google.com/o/oauth2/auth",
    "token_uri": "https://oauth2.googleapis.com/token",
    "auth_provider_x509_cert_url": "https://www.googleapis.com/oauth2/v1/certs",
    "client_secret": "YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET",
    "redirect_uris": ["http://localhost"]
  }
}

The first run opens a browser to sign in and saves ~/.google_client_token.json for later runs.

SharePoint/OneDrive. Save your Azure app registration as ~/.azure_client.json:

{
  "client_id": "YOUR_CLIENT_ID",
  "authority": "https://login.microsoftonline.com/consumers"
}

Use .../consumers for personal accounts or .../YOUR_TENANT_ID for an organization. The first run signs you in and caches the token in ~/.msal_token_cache.json.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
youtube-to-docs [VIDEO] [OPTIONS]

VIDEO is a YouTube URL, a video ID, a playlist ID (starts with PL), a channel handle (starts with @) or a comma-separated list of video IDs. Without it, the tool processes the sample video atmGAHYpf_c.

With no options, you get the transcript only. Add options for the outputs you want. Options marked bare can be used without a value to get the default shown.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option What it does Default -m, --model Speakers, Q&A, tags and summaries with an LLM. Comma-separate to compare models. Bare: gemini-3.5-flash-lite -t, --transcript Where the transcript comes from: youtube, or a speech-to-text model such as gemini-3.5-transcribe, gcp-chirp3 or aws-transcribe. youtube -i, --infographic An infographic, with alt text, from an image model. Comma-separate for one per model. Bare: gemini-3-pro-image --alt-text-model The LLM that writes the infographic alt text. The -m model --tts An audio summary. Format: {model}-{voice}, e.g. gemini-3.8-flash-lite-tts-Kore, gcp-chirp3-Kore or aws-polly-Ruth. None -cia, --combine-infographic-audio An MP4 that plays the audio summary over the infographic. Needs -i and --tts. Off -tr, --translate Translate every output. Format: {model}-{language}, e.g. gemini-3.5-flash-lite-es, aws-translate-es or gcp-translate-french. None -cc, --corrected-captions Corrected captions and audio description. See Corrected captions and audio description. Bare: gemini-4-argon-gemini-3.5-transcribe -fv, --from-video Also make the summary, speakers and Q&A from the video itself with Gemini: agentic, static or agentic,static. None -nys, --no-youtube-summary With an AI transcript, skip the extra summary of the YouTube transcript. Off -a, --all Use a model suite for summary, TTS and infographic (and set -nys): gemini-flash, gemini-pro, gemini-flash-pro-image, gcp-pro or anthropic-opus. None -pp, --post-process Extra columns from the transcript. Supports word count, e.g. '{"word count": ["apple", "banana"]}'. None -o, --outfile Where to save: a CSV path, workspace (w) or a Drive folder ID, sharepoint (s), hf, memory (m) or none (n). youtube-to-docs-artifacts/youtube-docs.csv --hugging-face-dataset The dataset for -o hf: a repo ID (username/my-dataset) or a name. The playlist title --verbose More detailed logs. Off -V, --version Show the version.

If you don't set -m, -cc turns on -m gemini-4-argon, and -i and -fv turn on -m gemini-3.5-flash-lite. Model names and prices are on the Pricing page, and speed and cost comparisons are on the Performance page.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Transcript only:

youtube-to-docs atmGAHYpf_c

Summaries, Q&A, speakers and tags with the default model:

youtube-to-docs atmGAHYpf_c -m

Compare two models across a playlist:

youtube-to-docs PLGKTTEqwhiHHWO-jdxM1KtzTbWo6h0Ycl -m gemini-3.5-flash-lite,vertex-claude-haiku-5-5

Transcribe the audio with Gemini 3.5 Transcribe (word timestamps and speaker labels in the SRT):

youtube-to-docs atmGAHYpf_c -t gemini-3.5-transcribe -m

A whole channel with infographics and audio summaries:

youtube-to-docs @mga-othercommittees6625 -m -i --tts gemini-3.8-flash-lite-tts-Kore

A video summary (the infographic with the audio summary):

youtube-to-docs atmGAHYpf_c -m -i --tts gemini-3.8-flash-lite-tts-Kore -cia

Everything in English and Spanish:

youtube-to-docs atmGAHYpf_c -m -i --tts gemini-3.8-flash-lite-tts-Kore -cia -tr gemini-3.5-flash-lite-es

Compare infographics from Gemini and Azure Foundry:

youtube-to-docs atmGAHYpf_c -m -i gemini-3-pro-image,foundry-gpt-image-2.5-sunburst

Accessible captions and audio description:

youtube-to-docs atmGAHYpf_c -cc

Save to Google Drive:

uvx --with "youtube-to-docs[all]" youtube-to-docs atmGAHYpf_c -m -o workspace

Count words in the transcript:

youtube-to-docs atmGAHYpf_c -pp '{"word count": ["apple", "banana"]}'

docs.title: Corrected captions and audio description
docs.text:
-cc / --corrected-captions makes a video accessible under WCAG 2.1 Level AA (1.2.2 Captions, 1.2.5 Audio Description) and Section 508, following the DCMP Captioning and Description Keys.

youtube-to-docs VIDEO_ID -cc

Without a value it uses gemini-4-argon-gemini-3.5-transcribe: the audio is transcribed with gemini-3.5-transcribe (word timestamps and speaker diarization) unless -t is set, and gemini-4-argon reads on-screen context from the video, corrects the captions and describes the visual information. A 3-hour meeting takes about 20 minutes and roughly $3 in API calls.

Other ways to run it:

# Correct the YouTube captions instead of transcribing
youtube-to-docs VIDEO_ID -cc gemini-4-argon-youtube

# Correct a GCP Chirp 3 transcript with a cheaper model
youtube-to-docs VIDEO_ID -t gcp-chirp3 -cc gemini-3.5-flash-lite-gcp-chirp3

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text: Output Folder Use … corrected captions (from {source}).srt srt-files/ Captions for YouTube or any player … corrected captions (from {source}).txt transcript-files/ The corrected captions as a plain-text transcript, a paragraph per speaker … captions (from {source}).vtt vtt-files/ Website: <track kind="captions"> (browsers don't read SRT) … descriptions.vtt vtt-files/ Website: <track kind="descriptions">, descriptions fitted into pauses (standard audio description, AA) … extended descriptions.vtt vtt-files/ Website: every description where its visual appears, for players that pause the video while reading (Able Player does by default; extended audio description, WCAG 1.2.7) … descriptive transcript.md descriptive-transcript-files/ The dialogue by speaker with every description; publish next to the video (WCAG 1.2.3 and 1.2.8) {id} - {title} - original video.mp4 video-files/ The source video for a website player … captioned and described video (from {source}).mp4 video-files/ A standalone accessible copy: captions burned in (white on an 80% opaque box) and the descriptions narrated in the pauses … player.html vtt-files/ An Able Player page with the original video, the WebVTT tracks and an interactive transcript, for checking them (it opens straight from disk) and as a template for a website … embed.html vtt-files/ The same player streaming the video from YouTube, with the tracks inside the page: a single file to paste into a site's embed box (e.g. Google Sites)

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Timing. The source SRT is aligned word by word with a second transcript of the same audio (the YouTube captions, or the STT transcript when correcting YouTube's). Cues with broken timestamps (for example, words returned minutes off) are re-timed from the second transcript.
  2. Speakers. The speaker of every cue is identified in ~20-minute windows from the diarization labels, the second transcript's speaker changes (>>), the times the video shows each person speaking, introductions, hand-offs and roles. Names come from on-screen name plates where available.
  3. Text. Sections of ~150 cues are corrected in parallel against the second transcript and the on-screen spellings: misheard words, names, organizations and acronyms, punctuation and capitalization, clean verbatim (fillers and stutters removed, false starts marked with em dashes), numbers, and non-speech sounds such as [laughter]. Speech missing from the source but present in the second transcript (often short replies) is restored. The model edits text by cue id and never writes timestamps, so long videos can't be truncated or drift out of sync.
  4. Layout. The corrected words are re-segmented into captions of at most two lines of 42 characters, 1–7 seconds long, broken at sentence and clause boundaries (not inside names or after articles). [Name] labels mark every change of speaker, crosstalk is placed at the nearest sentence break, quick exchanges share a two-line caption, and captions never overlap.
  5. Audio description. The video is downloaded and scanned for scene changes (new slides, changes of shot); the model looks at the frame at each change with the dialogue around it and writes a short spoken version and a full description of what isn't said aloud: slide titles, key on-screen text, the main figures in charts and tables, votes and video clips. Standard audio description is spoken only in pauses, so the short versions are fitted into pauses while their visual is on screen (most important first, shortened if needed), narrated with --tts (default gemini-3.8-flash-tts-Kore) and mixed in with the programme audio lowered. Nothing is narrated over speech; the extended track and the descriptive transcript carry every description.

Audio description needs a Gemini model; with other models -cc produces the captions only.

docs.title: Choosing the source
docs.text:
The format is -cc {model} or -cc {model}-{source}.

Source Behaviour Example STT model name Corrects the SRT from that STT run, transcribing it in the same run unless -t is set. -cc gemini-4-argon-gemini-3.5-transcribe youtube Corrects the YouTube SRT, using any STT SRT for the video as the second transcript. -cc gemini-4-argon-youtube Omitted Corrects the -t STT SRT, else the most recent AI SRT, else the YouTube SRT. -cc gemini-4-argon

If the requested source SRT doesn't exist (for example, -t youtube -cc), the available SRT is corrected instead, with a warning.

docs.title: Publishing
docs.text:
• Website: host the original video with captions.vtt and a descriptions track in a player that speaks descriptions, such as Able Player; the generated player.html shows the markup. Link the descriptive transcript next to the video.
  • Google Sites (or another site builder): open … embed.html in a text editor, copy all of it, and in Google Sites select Insert > Embed > Embed code and paste it. The video plays from YouTube with the corrected captions, the spoken descriptions and the interactive transcript; nothing else needs hosting. The descriptive transcript link is included when it is a full URL (such as a Google Doc, which must be shared with viewers). Embed boxes that sandbox the page without allow-same-origin stop the YouTube player from starting.
  • YouTube: upload the captioned and described video, or upload the original with the corrected SRT as its captions (YouTube has no description tracks, so audio description needs the described copy).

docs.title: Checking the WebVTT files
docs.text:
1. Validate them. Paste a .vtt file into the W3C WebVTT validator; it should report no errors.

  2. Play them. Open the … player.html file in a browser. Captions are on; select the Description button to hear the descriptions read aloud (the video pauses while each is read), and the Transcript button for an interactive transcript of the dialogue and descriptions. To hear the descriptions through a screen reader instead, add data-desc-reader="screenreader" to the <video> element and turn on NVDA, JAWS or VoiceOver.

    The page works straight from disk: browsers won't load .vtt files into a page opened that way, so it carries copies of the tracks and uses those. To load the .vtt files themselves, as a website would, serve the artifacts folder with a server that supports range requests (Python's built-in http.server doesn't, so the browser can't seek in a long video):

    cd youtube-to-docs-artifacts
uv run --no-project --with rangehttpserver python -m RangeHTTPServer 8080 --bind 127.0.0.1

    Then open http://127.0.0.1:8080/vtt-files/ and select the … player.html file.

  3. Spot-check timing. In VLC, open the original video and add the captions .vtt (Subtitle > Add Subtitle File...) to check that captions line up with the speech.

docs.title: Review and edit the outputs
docs.text:
youtube-to-docs is human-centered: the models write a first draft, and people review it and have the final say. Every output is a file you can edit (a Google Doc or Word file when saving to Google Drive or SharePoint), and the CSV lists where each one is saved.

Outputs that already exist aren't regenerated. When you run the same video again, the tool reads your edited files and uses them for any step that hasn't run yet. For example:

  1. Get the transcript only (the default): youtube-to-docs <url>.
  2. Fix the transcript in transcript-files/ (and the matching .srt in srt-files/ if you plan to make captions).
  3. Run again with the outputs you want, such as -m -i --tts gemini-3.8-flash-lite-tts-Kore or -cc. The summary, Q&A, infographic, audio and captions are built from your corrected transcript.

You can also edit a summary, Q&A, speakers or alt text file directly. On the next run, the edited text is loaded back into the CSV, and outputs made later, such as the infographic and audio, use it.

To make an output again, delete its file and remove the video's row from the CSV (or clear that output's columns), then run again. The tool finds your other files, including the edited transcript, by their file names.

docs.title: CSV columns
docs.text: The CSV has one row per video. Which columns appear depends on the options you use. In column names, {model} is the model that made the output, and {normalized_model} is the model name without prefixes like vertex- or date suffixes.

docs.title: Video details
docs.text:
• URL, Title, Description, Data Published, Channel, Duration: From YouTube.
  • Tags: The video's YouTube tags.
  • Tags {transcript} {model} model: Up to 5 tags generated from the transcript.
  • Transcript characters from youtube, Transcript characters from {model}: The length of each transcript.
  • Audio File: The downloaded audio, used for AI transcription.

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
Paths to the saved outputs. Translated outputs end in the language code, such as (es).

  • Transcript File {type}: The transcript. {type} is youtube generated, human generated or {model} generated.
  • SRT File {type}: The transcript as SRT captions.
  • Speakers File {model}, QA File {model}, Summary File {model}, One Sentence Summary File {model}, Tags File {model}: The text outputs. The Q&A table includes Timestamp and Timestamp URL columns that link to the moment in the video.
  • Summary Infographic File {model} {infographic_model}, Summary Infographic Alt Text File {model} {infographic_model}: The infographic and its alt text.
  • Summary Audio File {model} {tts_model} File: The audio summary.
  • Video File, Video File (lang): The infographic and audio summary video (-cia), in English and the translated language.
  • Corrected Captions File {model} from {source}, Transcript File {model} corrected from {source}, Captions VTT File {model} from {source}: The corrected captions as SRT, plain text and WebVTT (-cc).
  • Descriptions VTT File {model}, Extended Descriptions VTT File {model}, Descriptive Transcript File {model}: The audio description (-cc).
  • Original Video File, Captioned And Described Video File {model} from {source}, Player Page, Embed Page: The original video, the copy with captions burned in and descriptions narrated, the Able Player page, and its YouTube-streaming version for embedding in a site (-cc).
  • Post-process: word count({word}): How many times {word} appears in the transcript (case-insensitive, whole words), one column per word (-pp).

docs.title: Text and costs
docs.text:
• Speakers {model}: The speakers and their titles or roles, e.g. "Speaker 1 (Senator Katie Fry Hester, Co-Chair)". UNKNOWN marks a name or title that couldn't be found, and NaN means no speakers were found.
  • QA Text {model}, Summary Text {model}, One Sentence Summary {model}, Summary Infographic Alt Text {model} {infographic_model}: The text of each output.
  • {normalized_model} Speaker extraction cost ($), {normalized_model} QA cost ($), {normalized_model} tags cost from {transcript} ($): Estimated API cost of each step.
  • {normalized_model} summary cost ($): Speaker extraction plus summary.
  • Summary Infographic Cost {model} {infographic_model} ($), Summary Infographic Alt Text Cost {model} {infographic_model} ($): Infographic and alt text costs.
  • {normalized_model} STT cost ($): Speech-to-text cost. For gemini-3.5-transcribe the API reports audio input tokens but not output tokens, so this understates the cost.
  • {normalized_model} corrected captions cost from {source} ($): The -cc speaker identification and text correction, including thinking tokens. The on-screen context and the audio description are in {normalized_model} video context cost from video-agentic ($) and {normalized_model} audio description cost ($) (narration not included).

docs.title: Web app
docs.text:
The web app runs the same pipeline in your browser, with the logs streamed live and links to every output when it finishes.

uvx --with "youtube-to-docs[app]" youtube-to-docs-app

Then open http://localhost:8000.

Flag What it does Default --host Host to bind to. 0.0.0.0 exposes it on your network, and the app has no sign-in. 127.0.0.1 --port Port to bind to. 8000 --reload Reload when the code changes (for development). Off

The app builds the same arguments as the CLI and calls the same code, so the results match. It also has a REST API:

Method Endpoint Returns GET / The web page GET /api/model-suites The --all model suites POST /api/process Starts a job and returns its ID GET /api/jobs/{job_id} The job's status, output and artifacts GET /api/jobs/{job_id}/stream The job's logs as Server-Sent Events GET /api/artifacts/{path} A generated file

docs.title: MCP server
docs.text:
The tool also runs as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, so AI agents can call it. Its process_video tool takes the same options as the CLI.

The repository is a plugin for Claude Code and Antigravity. It adds the MCP server and a youtube-to-docs skill that tells the agent how to use it.

Claude CodeAntigravity 
claude plugin marketplace add DoIT-Artificial-Intelligence/youtube-to-docs
claude plugin install youtube-to-docs@youtube-to-docs

agy plugin install https://github.com/DoIT-Artificial-Intelligence/youtube-to-docs

Then ask in plain language, for example "Save a summary of https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KuPc06JgI_A". The agent asks for anything it needs, such as the model, and calls the tool. You can also run the skill directly: /youtube-to-docs <url> kitchen sink gemini pro spanish or /youtube-to-docs <url> captions.

Other MCP clients can start the server with:

uv run --no-project --with "youtube-to-docs[all]" python -m youtube_to_docs.mcp_server

from youtube_to_docs.transcript import fetch_transcript

transcript, is_generated, segments = fetch_transcript("atmGAHYpf_c")

docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
How youtube-to-docs works

youtube-to-docs turns videos into documents to search, share and hear. Here's how it works, in six steps.

1. Point it at YouTube

Start with a video link, a video ID, a playlist or a whole channel. Playlists and channels are expanded, and each video runs in turn.

2. Get the words

Next, it gets the words. By default, it uses YouTube's own captions. Or it transcribes the audio again with Gemini, Google Cloud or AWS. That gives real word timings and speaker labels. Either way, you get a transcript and a timed SRT file.

3. Let the model read

Then a language model of your choice reads the transcript. It can run on Gemini, Vertex AI, AWS Bedrock or Azure Foundry. It names the speakers and their titles. It pairs each question with its answer and a timestamp link. It writes a summary, a one-sentence summary and topic tags. Gemini can also watch the video, to read slides and name plates.

4. Turn it into media

From the summary, it can draw an infographic. Another model looks at the image and writes its alt text. It can read the summary aloud, and combine both into a video. And it can make everything again in a second language.

5. Make the video accessible

Add the -cc flag to make the original video accessible. Captions are corrected, and each speaker is named. They meet WCAG 2.1 Level AA and Section 508. Slides and on-screen text are described for blind viewers.

6. You stay in control

Every output is a file that you can review and edit. Run it again, and the later steps use your edits. A CSV lists every file and what each step cost. Save it all to your computer, Google Drive, SharePoint or Hugging Face.

Get started

Run it from the command line, the web app, or as a plugin for your AI assistant. One command takes you from a link to a full set of documents.
